title: The Trap of Teaching "Hacks": Why Shortcuts Are Not Solutions
author: Dario Emanuele
summary: Drawing on nearly eleven years of teaching and wide classroom observation, Dario Emanuele critiques pedagogical shortcuts, tricks designed to get students to the right answer without understanding the journey, focusing on the Butterfly Method for adding and subtracting fractions. He argues such hacks are arbitrary games with rules to be memorised rather than understood, failing on two fronts: they present no logic for why the steps work, and without that logical anchor they cannot be retained or reconstructed once the memory fades. He also names the engagement trap, warning that gamified compliance is often mistaken for genuine learning. His alternative is to teach methods as chained atoms, where understanding the first concept lets a student recall the rest, making learning sustainable rather than fragile.
points: Emanuele targets pedagogical shortcuts, especially with lower-attaining students, arguing they are arbitrary games whose rules must be memorised rather than understood.
The Butterfly Method for fractions is his exhibit: fast and correct, but with no inherent logic presented about why cross-multiplication works.
Without the anchor of logic, a hack becomes one more arbitrary rule that students forget and cannot reconstruct once the memory fades.
He warns of the engagement trap, mistaking gamified compliance or busy work for actual learning.
His alternative is teaching methods as chained atoms, where grasping the underlying logic lets students recall the rest without memorising a trick.
quotes: I’m talking about pedagogical shortcuts, tricks designed to help students get to the right answer without necessarily understanding the journey.
There is no inherent logic presented to the student regarding why they are cross-multiplying. It is a sterile memory exercise.
Without the anchor of logic (”the why”), the method becomes just one more arbitrary rule in a sea of academic content.
We often mistake busy work or “gamified” compliance for actual learning.
We should aim to teach methods that are like a set of chained atoms.
They don’t need to memorise a trick; they just need to think hard about the math.
